compression.title: Output: An Anthology of Computer-Generated Text, 1953–2023
compression.lede: is an anthology of seven decades of English-language outputs from implemented computer generation systems, 1953–2023, selected, introduced and edited by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram and Nick Montfort and co-published by Counterpath and the MIT Press in 2024; it sets the history of machine-written text against the claim that text generation began in Silicon Valley yesterday, and the archive holds it as a historical lineage of machine output whose crediting of each output its publisher's page leaves unrecorded.

sentences.text: Output: An Anthology of Computer-Generated Text, 1953–2023 is an anthology of seven decades of English-language outputs from computer generation systems, chronicling the history of machine-written texts made long before ChatGPT, and both censuses of the archive that hold it record it as a historical lineage of machine output.
Its co-editor gives the span as seven decades of computer-generated text, "beginning before the term “artificial intelligence” was even coined".

The publisher's page sets the book against a discussion of computer-generated text that "largely omits the long history of work in this area—text generation, as it happens, was not invented yesterday in Silicon Valley", and the anthology "aims to correct that omission".
It was selected, introduced and edited by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram and Nick Montfort, co-editors after more than four years of work, and published jointly by Counterpath and the MIT Press.

Bertram is the author of Travesty Generator, a book of computational poetry longlisted for the 2020 National Book Award for Poetry, and directs the MFA in Creative Writing program at the University of Maryland.

Montfort is a poet and artist who uses computation as his medium, Professor of Digital Media at MIT and Principal Investigator in the Center for Digital Narrative at the University of Bergen; he founded and edits Counterpath's Using Electricity, a series of computer-generated books, and The Truelist (Counterpath, 2017), under his name, is a computer-generated book-length poem produced by a one-page computer program.

The archive's field survey places both editors in the procedural lineage, which "established that composition can be delegated to systems": Montfort among its living masters, the Using Electricity series at Counterpath named with his work, and Bertram's Travesty Generator as the book that "turned procedural generation into an interrogation of algorithmic anti-Blackness".
Its short title is Output; the publisher's title line prints the first editor as "Lillian Yvonne-Bertram" and its body as "Lillian-Yvonne Bertram", and the census records follow the body.

The sources part on the edition: Counterpath's page gives October 2024, 500 pages, 7″ x 9″, $40.00 and ISBN 978-0262549813, the particulars the authorship census carries for its holder, while the MIT Press listing gives a paperback under the same ISBN published November 5, 2024, at 504 pages, 7 x 9 in, with 41 black-and-white illustrations.

Montfort's announcement is dated 2024-11-05 and counts "200 selections in the 500-page book", and the MIT Press listing names the MIT Press Bookstore, Penguin Random House, Amazon, Barnes and Noble and Bookshop as sellers.

The outputs span many types of creative writing and include text from research systems along with reports and utilitarian texts: the work of "artists, poets, and other sorts of writers who have taken computing and code into their own hands", rhetorical generation, story generation systems based on cognitive research, "real news" generation, hoaxes and humor.

An overall introduction by the two editors stands with an introduction to each excerpt and longer introductions to each fine-grained genre of text generation, and the excerpts are organized by fine-grain genre, among them conversations, humor, letters, poetry, prose and sentences.

Bibliographic references allow readers to learn more about outputs and systems, which the layer census reads as tying each output back to its system and publication; the records give what it answers as which implemented systems produced which outputs, as the editors selected them, and where each output's published source is found.

Output is "first and foremost a collection of outputs to be encountered by readers" and, though it could serve as a reference book, is "designed to be readable and to be read"; its editors hope it will be a sourcebook for academics and students and a way for general readers to learn about innovations in computing and writing.
Its admission rule reads: "Purposefully excluded are human–computer collaborations that were conceptually defined but not implemented as a computer system."

The authorship census reads the rule as what constitutes the record as output of implemented systems, and both censuses mark what the anthology is not: a record of contemporary LLM co-writing alone, since it spans 1953 to 2023 with research systems, reports and utilitarian texts, nor a collection of conceptual collaborations, which it excludes.

The authorship census asks "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and holds the anthology under machine participation in authorship and the archives of experimental writing, answering which implemented systems produced which outputs from 1953 to 2023 as the editors select them.

Its answer from the publisher's page: the record keeps the editors' selection and introductions, and the page does not say whether an output stands under a system's name, a programmer's or both, how a given output's authorship is attributed, or whether any example is contemporary LLM co-writing.

The archive reads the page as setting the book against the claim that text generation began recently and as admitting only implemented systems, a lineage of machine output, and reads the anthology as a historical map of generated text whose attribution practice (system, programmer, editor) the saved page leaves unrecorded.

The archive's account of heteronymy places three neighbouring forms at its operational boundary: "Ordinary editing, where the editor's contribution is supportive rather than function-constitutive", "Machine assistance, where the AI's contribution is not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance", and "Collaborative authorship, where multiple civil bearers contribute but no distinct heteronym is constituted".

The archive's definitions of training-layer literature set it apart from the class of machine-written text by the direction of authorship: "AI-generated content is writing whose author is a language model", AI-generated poetry "has a machine writer and a human reader", procedural or computational poetry takes the machine as method, and training-layer literature has a human writer and a machine reader and "composes for computation" where computational poetics "Analyzes text computationally".

The layer census asks "How is literature addressed to a receiving apparatus, what does that apparatus make from it, and how can transmission, transformation and provenance be inspected across later reception?", and holds the anthology under field history and machine composition, as the field history of generative transformation with each output traced to its system by bibliographic reference.

Its object is what generation systems made, from implemented systems only; the saved page says nothing of what the systems read or were trained on, nor whether any output was composed for a machine reader, and the layer census marks it as neither a record of training nor evidence of composition addressed to a machine reader.

The archive reads Output as the edited field history of the direction it writes TM→, "machine-after-reception → new artifact", seven decades of what implemented generation systems emitted, and as the procedural lineage its field survey names in Montfort's Using Electricity series and Bertram's Travesty Generator.

The same account separates two questions every such output poses, "Did the machine write something new? and Did the machine tell the truth about where it came from?", having found hallucination "too coarse a category because it treated novel composition and false provenance as the same defect".

It is a print book, with no licence stated on the publisher's page, and the two census records part on its lifecycle: the authorship census gives it as active, published October 2024 and offered for sale on 2026-11-01, and the layer census as ended, a single published volume with no later edition announced.

Montfort's announcement lists launches, talks and events from November 2024 to April 2025, among them a European launch with the editors, Scott Rettberg and Tegan Pyke at the University of Bergen's Center for Digital Narrative on 13 December, which "was streamed & recorded and is available to view on YouTube".

The Center's video of the book, "Output: An Anthology of Computer", introduces Montfort in its card's transcription as one who "uses computation litary art" and "a PI in the center" with "many books that include computerenerated books".
Wikipedia has no article under its title, a search of article space returns no result for it, and the articles on its two editors do not name it.

Google's Overview at the title carries a card stating that the response "uses data provided by Google's Knowledge Graph", which Google describes as "our database of billions of facts about people, places, and things", its facts drawn from "a variety of sources that compile factual information".

Both census records rest on the Counterpath page alone: the MIT page at cmsw.mit.edu failed at fetch with a TLS certificate error and stands unread, and the anthology itself, its contents, introductions and bibliography, was not read.

The registry enters the anthology as external, "Not the archive's", and the records set it beside ReRites, in which Montfort writes a response essay, and beside The Readers Project, whose How It Is in Common Tongues Montfort noted as a Radical Book of 2012.

Asked for the book by its title at a new address, the Overview gives its publishers, date, length, editors, range, genres, scope, an award and its prices, mostly from the MIT Press page, and names both editors, both publishers and the ISBN; the Capture Registry reads it as an accurate composition of the book as a catalogue item whose date, length and price differ from the Counterpath page the census rests on.

The registry finds the exclusion rule loosened, its condition dropped and "pure" added in "deliberately excluding pure human-computer conceptual collaborations", and the book's argument against a recent origin of machine text uncarried, the years given without the correction.

Its follow-up names two systems under their makers' names, "Joseph E. Grimes' 1963 Fairy Tale Generator" and "Alison Knowles' The House of Dust", and the registry records that how the book itself credits these outputs is in no saved source.

The registry records "200 selections" and the Hayles Award mention as on no saved source and the timeframe line as reading "from 1953 to 1953–2023"; the co-editor's announcement, the third card on the Overview's rail, states "There are 200 selections in the 500-page book".

CAP-1-06.quote: The innocent reading first. Asked for the book by its title, the Overview gives its publishers, date, length, editors, range, genres, scope, an award and its prices, mostly from the MIT Press page.

CAP-1-10.quote: Both editors and both publishers named; the ISBN on the MIT Press card.

CAP-1-07.quote: An accurate composition of the book as a catalogue item, taken from MIT Press, whose date, length and price differ from the Counterpath page the census rests on. The exclusion rule loses its condition, and the book's argument against a recent origin of machine text is absent.

CAP-1-02.quote: THE EDITION'S PARTICULARS. The composition and its MIT Press card: 'Pub date: November 5, 2024 504 pp.', paperback '$45.00'. Counterpath's page, the census row's source: 'October 2024', '500 pgs.', '$40.00; 7″ x 9″'. The ISBN agrees ('Paperback ISBN: 9780262549813'; 'ISBN 978-0262549813'). The census row's holder field carries Counterpath's month and price.

CAP-1-08.quote: 'OUTPUT: AN ANTHOLOGY OF COMPUTER-GENERATED TEXT' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE BOOK AT ITS GRAIN FROM MIT PRESS; ITS EXCLUSION RULE LOOSENED; ITS ARGUMENT AGAINST A RECENT ORIGIN OF TEXT GENERATION NOT CARRIED

CAP-1-03.quote: THE EXCLUSION LOOSENED. Counterpath: 'Purposefully excluded are human–computer collaborations that were conceptually defined but not implemented as a computer system.' The composition: 'deliberately excluding pure human-computer conceptual collaborations'. The condition that does the excluding, a collaboration never implemented as a system, is dropped, and 'pure' is added; the census row reads this rule as what constitutes the record as output of implemented systems.

CAP-1-04.quote: THE PURPOSE NOT CARRIED. Counterpath sets the book against a recent origin: 'text generation, as it happens, was not invented yesterday in Silicon Valley', 'created long before ChatGPT', and the anthology 'aims to correct that omission'. The composition gives the years without the correction.

CAP-1-05.quote: ATTRIBUTION BY POSSESSIVE. The follow-up names two systems by their makers, 'Joseph E. Grimes' 1963 Fairy Tale Generator' and 'Alison Knowles' The House of Dust', each system under a person's name. The census row records the book's attribution practice (system, programmer, editor) as unrecorded on the saved page; how the book itself credits these outputs is not in any saved source.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE BOOK AT ITS GRAIN. Editors, range and genres agree with Counterpath's page ('organized by fine-grain genre including conversations, humor, letters, poetry, prose, and sentences'). The timeframe line reads 'from 1953 to 1953–2023'. '200 selections' and the Hayles Award mention are on no saved source.
